item.title: Jilin University lab leverages AI to study ancient Chinese scripts and relics
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-12
A member of the Key Laboratory of Ancient Chinese Script, Culture Relics and Artificial Intelligence of Jilin University observes details of pottery inscriptions of the Warring States Period (475 BC-221 BC) at Jilin University in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Sept. 2, 2026. Established in 2023, the Key Laboratory of Ancient Chinese Script, Culture Relics and Artificial Intelligence of Jilin University brings together researchers in the fields of paleography, archaeology, history, artificial intelligence, etc. With oracle bone inscriptions, bronze inscriptions, Warring States scripts, and Qin and Han scripts as core subjects for research, the laboratory sorts and catalogs scripts and culture relics in a systematic manner, and facilitates its work with artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. "We hope to bridge the past and the present via AI, and accelerate research of ancient characters with a 'smart engine,' and 'wake up' the ancient books and documents that have been dormant for ages," said Li Chuntao, director of the laboratory. item.title: China's "golden outer ring" highways fuel new economic corridors
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-12
SHENYANG, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- A scenic coastal highway in China has left a deep impression on Lee Jae-jae, a cycling enthusiast from the Republic of Korea (ROK). Lee was among a group of 49 cyclists that visited Dandong, a border city in northeast China's Liaoning Province, aboard a passenger-and-cargo ferry from Incheon, ROK. "Dandong has a very comfortable climate and beautiful roadside scenery. The cycling paths, rest areas and other facilities are well-equipped, making for a smooth and pleasant riding experience," he said. The Dandong section of the G228 national highway offers just a glimpse of the many attractions along the emerging "golden outer ring." China plans to fully link three national highways -- the G219, G331 and G228 -- creating an ultra-long ring route that traces China's borders and coastal areas during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). Stretching over 26,000 kilometers if connected, nearly two-thirds of the equatorial circumference, the route traverses a diverse tapestry of landscapes and tourist attractions, from coastlines and snow-capped mountains to glaciers, grasslands, deserts, lakes and border crossings. It is poised to become a major corridor driving tourism and broader industrial development. Dandong, where the G331 and G228 begin, is already reaping considerable benefits from its location. "Two national highways pass through our village, attracting a constant flow of self-driving travelers and border-tourism lovers throughout the year," said Wang Chunhai, Party chief of Hushan Village of Dandong. Leveraging this advantage, the village transformed its idle land into recreational vehicle (RV) campsites and homestays, drawing praise from visitors while generating additional collective income for the village, according to Wang. "Many visitors have told me that the drive from Dandong along the Yalu River offers beautiful scenery the whole way," said Zheng Jinhua, a resident of Guoyuan Village in adjacent Jilin Province, adding that a growing number of villagers have opened homestays or started to sell local farm produce to visitors. Statistics show that the G331, which traces the country's northern border, welcomed more than 2 million tourists in the first half of this year. For residents of border villages along the route, tourism has become a source of livelihood at their doorstep, with many investing in homestays, running specialty restaurants or selling local agricultural products. Serving as a principal artery along China's western and southern frontier, G219 is home to a remarkable diversity of ecological and geographical landscapes, winding through the Taklamakan Desert, China's largest, and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, widely known as the "roof of the world." In June, the China Tourist Attractions Association, joined by state-owned cultural and tourism groups from Xinjiang, Xizang, Yunnan and other provincial-level regions, initiated preparations for a coordinated development mechanism for the G219 cultural and tourism industry, with the goal of better aligning cultural and tourism resources along the route. "As China's longest border road, G219 boasts abundant cultural and tourism resources along the way, such as snow-capped mountains, glaciers and grasslands, which can directly fuel tourism, rural revitalization and border stability and prosperity," said Liu Rangqun, general manager of Xinjiang Culture & Tourism Investment Group Co., Ltd. Meanwhile, the G228, which stretches along China's eastern coastline, links coastal ports and forms a transportation and logistics channel connecting land borders to coastal ports, noted Li Hongchang, a professor at Beijing Jiaotong University. "By organically integrating transportation hubs, it helps drive the all-round economic and social development of the areas it passes through," Li said. Along the route in Dandong, for example, cross-border e-commerce transaction volume posted a double-digit increase over the past year. A well-developed road network can transform what was once a transportation periphery into a frontier for openness, said Ma Jiangbo, deputy director of the China economic research center under the China Institute for Innovation & Development Strategy. An integrated network, rather than three separate channels, can further reduce cross-border logistics costs and make China's industrial layout more balanced, Ma added. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, the country has planned to work faster to boost its strength in transportation and improve the modern integrated transportation system, raising the completion rate of the main framework of the national integrated multidimensional transportation network to 95 percent. ■

item.title: Economic Watch: From owning to experiencing: services trade fair mirrors China's rise as service consumption powerhouse
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-12
BEIJING, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- With just a tap on a screen, Ms. Wang watched herself instantly transformed from a modern fashionista into Mu Guiying, her favorite Peking Opera character from centuries ago. This AI-powered experience was presented by the Jingju Theater Company of Beijing at the ongoing 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS). Wang, a longtime Peking Opera fan and a first-time CIFTIS visitor from Beijing, remembered how getting an opera costume photo or video once meant tracking down a specialized studio in the city. It was a process that was both expensive and time-consuming. "Now, with AI technology showcased at the services trade fair, everyone can easily realize their Peking Opera dream." Beyond this immersive experience, the 2026 CIFTIS, running from Sept. 9 to 13 at Shougang Park in Beijing, has brought together 413 exhibitors at the themed exhibition area for culture and tourism services, showcasing emerging models of cultural and tourism integration. But AI's reach goes beyond the culture and tourism pavilion. Throughout the fair, humanoid robots offer bilingual explanations, brain-computer interfaces create digital paintings, and AI 360-degree photo booths generate blockbuster-style videos in real time -- all pointing to a broader trend: China's consumption is upgrading from goods to experiences. SERVICE CONSUMPTION ON THE RISE For the first time, this year's CIFTIS set up a "China Services" exhibition zone, showcasing more than 140 cases covering 12 major areas of services trade. Nearly 40 percent of the cases feature core technologies such as AI, large models and intelligent agents. The "China Services" pavilion also shines a light on new business models and scenarios in the world of services trade. Exhibits range from age-friendly solutions designed to bridge the digital divide, to smart childcare platforms that provide integrated health management from birth through preschool. Behind the bustling booths lies huge growth momentum and potential for China's services sector, said Wang Min, president of the China General Chamber of Commerce, at a forum during the fair. Wang noted that people's consumption focus has been shifting from being dominated by goods to a balanced emphasis on both goods and services, with digital technologies spawning new business forms such as emotional consumption, immersive experiences and cross-border services consumption. Official statistics echo the sentiments of many speakers like Wang at the CIFTIS. In the first seven months of this year, retail sales of services rose 5 percent year on year, outpacing growth in retail sales of consumer goods by 3.9 percentage points. The growth came as China's per capita spending on services reached 13,602 yuan (about 2,009 U.S. dollars) in 2025, accounting for 46.1 percent of total per capita consumption expenditure. With the steady growth of people's disposable income and improvements in the domestic consumption environment, Chinese consumers' spending on services is expected to further grow in the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), analysts noted. According to a government plan issued by the State Council in April, the country aims to elevate the total scale of the services industry to over 100 trillion yuan by 2030. To unlock this potential, authorities have rolled out a series of policies and initiatives. In July, China released its first five-year plan dedicated exclusively to expanding consumption, further positioning service consumption as a priority. The plan calls for steadily raising the share of per capita service consumption expenditure, with targeted support for elderly care, childcare, culture and tourism, health and sports services. For Li Jun, director of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under the Ministry of Commerce, the services sector's leap toward the 100-trillion-yuan mark represents not simple expansion, but a systemic upgrade in structure and growth drivers. "The popularity of the culture, tourism, education and sports exhibition areas at CIFTIS is a vivid illustration of this trend," Li said. CHINESE SERVICES OFFER GLOBAL OPPORTUNITIES At the sports services exhibition area, "China Hawk Eye," a Chinese-developed sports system, became a popular attraction among professional fair visitors and sports fans. With multiple high-speed cameras capturing ball trajectories from different angles and algorithms reconstructing disputed moments into visualized 3D images, the system now serves multiple international professional events. The system exemplifies how China has posted rapid growth in services trade. Latest official data showed that in the first seven months of this year, the country's services trade totaled nearly 4.45 trillion yuan, up 8.3 percent year on year. In particular, knowledge-intensive services increased 6.6 percent to 1.96 trillion yuan, accounting for 44.1 percent of total services trade. In a video address to the Global Trade in Services Summit, a landmark event during CIFTIS, World Intellectual Property Organization Director General Daren Tang hailed China's rapid growth in services trade, saying that the country's strong exports of knowledge-intensive services are supported by the intellectual property and innovation ecosystem. A report released at CIFTIS on Wednesday also highlighted the growing strength of China's services brands. China ranks second globally with 21 brands in the world's 100 most valuable trade in services brands, with a combined worth of 876.8 billion U.S. dollars, according to the report, "Trade in Services 100 2026," by brand valuation consultancy Brand Finance. Alex Haigh, managing director of Brand Finance Asia Pacific, said by leveraging the synergies of digital platforms, communications networks and large financial institutions, Chinese trade in services brands are rising rapidly, reflecting a new trend of extending "Made in China" to "China services" and "China brands." China's efforts to actively promote services trade and open up its services sector wider are creating more opportunities for countries and businesses around the world, experts said. Noting that international services trade facilitation still faces barriers, Zhao Ping, president of the Academy of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, called for further leveraging the role of CIFTIS to promote trade and investment liberalization and facilitation. ■

item.title: BRICS key to Global South representation, scholar says
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-12
"Rather than replacing existing global institutions, BRICS seeks to strengthen the principles of dialogue, sovereign equality, mutual respect and cooperation among nations," said Balew Demissie, a senior consultant at the Policy Studies Institute of Ethiopia, adding that the group is more representative of and responsive to the interests and aspirations of the Global South, thereby contributing to a fairer and more genuinely multipolar world order. ADDIS ABABA, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- The BRICS is playing an increasingly important role in safeguarding genuine multilateralism and international rules by fostering a more balanced, inclusive and representative international order, an expert has said. "BRICS is a venue for partnership, collaboration, and dialogue," Balew Demissie, a senior consultant at the Policy Studies Institute of Ethiopia, recently told Xinhua. "It promotes multilateralism, not unilateralism." He said the group is playing an increasingly prominent role in "keeping the balance, inclusivity and representation" within the wider multilateral governance structure, where no single country or group dominates global decision-making. "Rather than replacing existing global institutions, BRICS seeks to strengthen the principles of dialogue, sovereign equality, mutual respect and cooperation among nations," he said, adding that the group is more representative of and responsive to the interests and aspirations of the Global South, thereby contributing to a fairer and more genuinely multipolar world order. BRICS, with its expanded membership, provides a platform for emerging economies across the globe to have a stronger voice in global decision-making, particularly on issues such as trade, development, finance, climate change, peace and security, Demissie said. He noted that through organizations such as the New Development Bank, BRICS also contributes to diversifying global economic and financial partnerships, while serving as a constructive counterweight to unilateralism by promoting "greater openness, predictability, cooperation and inclusiveness in international economic relations." Meanwhile, he highlighted China's contribution to global development through its role in the BRICS and through other collaborative initiatives, such as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the Global Development Initiative. "Ethiopia has benefited immensely from the BRI in different aspects, including infrastructure, health, education, agriculture and rural revitalization," the scholar said. He argued that China's continued opening-up and inclusive trade policies provide significant opportunities for Global South countries by expanding access to one of the world's largest and most dynamic markets. China's economic approach "encourages stronger South-South cooperation and helps Global South countries diversify their trading and development partnerships, contributing to a more open, interconnected, and balanced global economy, while creating jobs and attracting necessary expertise," he noted. To navigate current and future global uncertainties, BRICS should deepen collaboration in trade and investment, infrastructure, energy, education, digital technology and skills development, while expanding market access for small and medium-sized enterprises, he said. Demissie also highlighted the critical importance of maintaining unity and coordination as the group expands and becomes increasingly diverse, requiring sustained dialogue, mutual understanding and flexible approaches to build consensus among members. ■

item.title: Xinhua Commentary: BRICS opens up new possibilities for more dynamic Global South
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-12
by Xinhua writer Liu Bowei BEIJING, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- When the BRICS cooperation mechanism was formally launched in 2006, it opened a new chapter for cooperation among major emerging economies. Two decades on, BRICS has, through the ebbs and flows of the global economy, expanded through multiple rounds of enlargement and broadened the scope of its cooperation. This evolution has ushered in a new era of greater BRICS cooperation, better reflecting the growing weight and aspirations of the Global South. When BRICS leaders prepare to gather for this year's summit in New Delhi, India, the mechanism is playing a greater role in amplifying the collective voice of emerging economies, and expanding practical cooperation amid a changing international landscape beset by raging protectionism and economic fragmentation. Its growing weight is reflected in its economic and demographic scale. BRICS countries now account for approximately 40 percent of global GDP at purchasing power parity and nearly half of the world's population. Data released by the UN Trade and Development in March showed that the intra-BRICS merchandise trade has expanded more than 13-fold since 2003, and exports reached 1.17 trillion U.S. dollars in 2024. BRICS, however, is more than an economic force. Its growing significance lies in how countries with different development paths are pooling their strengths in resources, industry and technology to advance shared development. A prominent area is financing. For many developing economies, access to affordable, long-term funding remains critical to turning development ambitions into reality. The New Development Bank (NDB), headquartered in Shanghai, has helped provide such an option by mobilizing resources for infrastructure and sustainable development projects. Figures released by the bank showed that by the end of the first quarter of 2026, the NDB had approved 42.9 billion dollars in financing for 140 projects. Covering such areas as infrastructure, clean energy and digital transformation, these projects address the pressing development needs of Global South countries while echoing the priorities highlighted by the theme of the forthcoming BRICS Summit, "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability." The ever-evolving BRICS cooperation is also helping developing countries gain new growth momentum. In recent years, BRICS cooperation has been expanding into areas like renewable energy, digital infrastructure, scientific and technological innovation. A case in point is the BRICS Partnership on New Industrial Revolution Innovation Center in Xiamen, which was established in 2020 to provide a platform for cooperation in digitalization, advanced manufacturing and technological innovation. These efforts point to the broader value of BRICS: it is not simply giving the Global South a stronger voice, but creating practical opportunities for countries to access financing, technology and cooperation suited to their development needs. Such collaboration helps explain BRICS' growing appeal to countries seeking greater opportunities to participate and cooperate. As a founding member, China has contributed not only by building platforms for practical cooperation, but also by supporting greater openness and broader participation to promote high-quality cooperation within an expanded BRICS. Some in the West portray BRICS as a rival bloc seeking to build a parallel order. Yet this claim bears little resemblance to reality. BRICS stands for openness, inclusiveness and mutual benefit, not confrontation or exclusion. That is fundamentally different from the exclusive blocs championed by some Western countries, and a key reason behind the growing vitality of BRICS. Looking ahead, BRICS is poised to embark on its third "golden decade" after 20 years of growth and transformation. By rising up to the challenges of the times, BRICS countries can help shape a more equal and orderly multipolar world and a more universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, and, in doing so, write a new chapter of solidarity and cooperation across the Global South. ■
